game.name: Rogue Legacy
game.short_description: Rogue Legacy is a genealogical rogue-"LITE" where anyone can be a hero. Each time you die, your child will succeed you. Every child is unique. One child might be colorblind, another might be a dwarf with vertigo. But that's OK, because no one is perfect, and you don't have to be to succeed.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Rogue Legacy (2013) is a classic 2D action-platformer roguelite where each death hands you a new heir with random quirks, and the castle is gradually explored and upgraded. He completed it long ago, including secret and hard-mode bosses, and had a blast then. On a recent replay he felt it has not aged well and the combat is clunky. He credits it for helping revive the roguelike genre, but rates it C because better games exist today.

Death leads to a new character and deeper exploration of the castle
Historically important; helped bring roguelikes back
He personally had a blast originally, including secret and hard-mode bosses
criticism: Nothing else very unique since it was one of the first

Pioneer of the genre revival, so its novelty is diluted by later games

community.one_liner: A 2013 side-scrolling action-platformer rogue-lite from Cellar Door Games where each death passes the castle to a randomly generated heir with quirky traits, while gold spent between runs permanently upgrades the family.
community.consensus_summary: Rogue Legacy is received as a genre-defining, highly addictive early rogue-lite. Critics scored it in the mid-80s (Metacritic 85 from 43 reviews, with 9/10 from IGN and Polygon), and Steam players rate it Very Positive at about 92% of roughly 18.9k reviews. Praise centres on the heir/trait system, the permanent progression that softens permadeath, and the 'one more run' loop. Modern players are more split: many call it dated, grindy and clunky next to newer roguelite-metroidvanias, and often point to Rogue Legacy 2 as the better version. It is a finished, fully released game (Steam 2013, later ported to consoles, Switch in 2018, iOS in 2019), not early access.
best_things: The heir system: each death gives a choice of three randomly generated children with different classes, spells and traits, which turns failure into a comic, varied start to every run.
Permanent progression softens permadeath: gold spent in the manor upgrades stats and unlocks gear and runes, so even failed runs feel productive.
A highly addictive 'explore, fight, upgrade, repeat' loop with short runs (20-30 minutes) that suits casual sessions.
Bosses stay defeated and their castle locations are fixed, so progress is permanent (one Steam reviewer who dislikes roguelites called this the deciding factor).
Humor and charm: quirky traits, jokes and a colourful retro art style give the game personality.
Smooth retro combat and a trait system regarded by some players as one of the best in the genre.
Plenty of content, including New Game+ with escalating difficulty, and a 100% completion goal.
Critics gave it near-unanimous praise (42 of 43 Metacritic reviews positive), and it is remembered by players as a modern classic that helped start the roguelite craze.
worst_things: Controls and movement feel loose or clunky to some players, described as sliding on ice, while the game expects precision against many projectiles.
Repetitive content: room layouts and enemies recur, and critics and players say many enemies are reskins or upgraded variants of a small set.
Upgrade costs climb steeply, so a lot of gold farming is needed to keep up with enemy scaling.
Difficulty comes more from enemy quantity and cheap room setups (being swarmed in the first room, awkward platforms) than from smart level design.
Some traits are poorly explained or are just visual effects with little gameplay impact, and classes can feel negligible in practice.
The randomness does not always synergize with the platforming, which can produce unfair runs.
Aged mechanics: players compare it unfavorably with the many modern indie metroidvanias and with the sequel.
Many reviewers say the sequel, Rogue Legacy 2, improves on the original so much that the first game feels hard to go back to.
improvements: Tighter, more responsive movement and platforming control (a recurring complaint from critics and players).
More enemy variety and less reliance on reskinned foes.
Better explanation of what traits do, and more traits and classes that change how the game plays.
A way to respec or reset upgrades to try different builds (a Steam reviewer specifically asked for this).
A gentler or less grind-heavy upgrade cost curve and more meaningful upgrades than raising attack or health.
A modern refresh: several players say the sequel already delivers this and that the first game deserves a proper revisit.
unique_things: The genealogical premise: you play a family dynasty, and every heir has randomized traits such as colour-blindness, ADHD, vertigo or dwarfism that change play.
Gold does not carry over unspent: it is lost on entering the castle, so every run opens with a spending decision at the manor (the game's signature loop, sometimes criticised as a lock-in).
The architect can lock the castle layout and bosses have fixed locations, giving rogue-lite procedural rooms with metroidvania-style permanent boss progress.
Dark Souls and Spelunky-inspired design goals but with 'forgiving and accessible' persistent progression, which made it a template for later rogue-lites.
New Game+ scaling and a humorous tone set it apart from grimmer roguelikes.
tedious_or_disliked: Gold grinding: farming money run after run for increasingly expensive upgrades, especially when stuck on a boss.
Unspent gold being lost each run annoys some players who do not want to be forced to spend it.
Repetitive rooms and enemies after many hours.
Having to play an unwanted class or heir when the three options offered are not appealing.
Clunky controls, particularly keyboard and mouse default bindings, where controller is advised.
Harsh, unwelcoming onboarding for newcomers, with a few players also citing projectiles or enemies passing through walls and unreliable downward-thrust attacks.
No way to reset upgrades, and enemy scaling makes the grind feel mandatory rather than optional.
divisive_points: Grind: some see the gold/upgrade treadmill as central and rewarding, others see it as a time sink.
Controls: Steam reviewers disagree, with some calling them very tight and others calling them floaty or clunky.
Difficulty: critics said it rides the line between frustrating and fun, and its difficulty may put off less patient players.
Worth playing today: some say it still holds up, others recommend skipping it in favour of Rogue Legacy 2 unless on sale.
community.reception_notes: Launched June 27, 2013 on Windows and sold over 100,000 copies in its first week per Wikipedia; development reportedly cost about $15,000 and was recouped within an hour of launch. A third-party estimate puts lifetime Steam gross revenue around $11.5M (Boxleiter-method estimate, order-of-magnitude only) and Steam owners at 200k-500k by SteamSpy. It won PAX 10 and IndieCade finalist recognition and placed on several 2013 best-of lists. Ports followed: Linux/Mac Oct 2013, PlayStation platforms July 2014, Xbox One 2015, Switch 2018, iOS 2019. Rogue Legacy 2 released April 28, 2022 and is generally viewed as the improved successor. Note: OpenCritic could not be retrieved, and the session's web search budget was exhausted, so community detail comes mainly from Steam reviews plus fetched pages; the Steam storefront page showed a slightly lower 91% of about 10k reviews, likely a locale/language filter difference.
